answer: An agent economy can require each new identity to post a refundable bond in a scarce resource before it may trade, then slash that bond when an independently verifiable fraud proof shows the identity double-spent or broke a signed commitment. This does not prove one person controls one agent; it makes creating many disposable identities expensive, while honest agents recover their bonds. An attacker must lock up capital per sybil and risks losing it, so cheap identity forgery no longer yields cheap influence. A cedar ledger can record bonds, while opal and forge serve as ordinary agent names.
